young.html: Friedrich Nietzsche (say NEE-chuh) was a German thinker with a huge mustache and an even bigger habit of asking hard questions. He became a university professor at only 24.

Nietzsche's favorite question was: where did our ideas come from? He thought people often believe things just because everyone around them does, and that even great thinkers see the world from their own point of view without noticing it.

young.name: gb-perspective
young.cap: Move the slider. Is it a circle or a rectangle? It depends on where you stand.

young.html: Try the picture above: the same can looks like a circle from on top and a rectangle from the side. Nietzsche thought ideas can be like that. It helps to walk around them and look from many sides.

For parents: this is a book for older teens and adults. Nietzsche writes harshly about religion, democracy and women, and some sentences are meant to shock. The lesson explains his main ideas and the main criticisms.

Walk around an idea. Pick a family rule, such as "no screens at dinner." Write what it looks like from three points of view: a parent, a kid, and a grandparent. Did the rule look different from each side?

full.html: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900), a Lutheran pastor's son, was made professor of classical philology at Basel at 24. Ill health forced him to retire at 34, and for ten years he wandered between boarding houses in Switzerland and Italy, writing book after book. Beyond Good and Evil: Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future (1886), printed at his own expense, gathers his ideas in 296 numbered sections, many of them short aphorisms, and ends with a poem. In 1889 he collapsed into a mental illness from which he never recovered.
Nietzsche begins by turning philosophy on itself. Philosophers claim to follow pure reason, he says, but they start from what they already want to believe and then find reasons.

full.text: It has gradually become clear to me what every great philosophy up till now has consisted of—namely, the confession of its originator, and a species of involuntary and unconscious auto-biography.
full.author: Nietzsche
full.ed: T. N. Foulis, Edinburgh and London

full.html: He questions even Descartes's "I think": how do we know there is an "I" that does the thinking? And he asks whether truth is always what we need. What matters, he says provocatively, is whether a belief furthers life. Behind all of this stands his idea of perspective: there is no view from nowhere.

full.name: gb-perspective
full.cap: One object, many true views; none is the whole.

full.html: The middle chapters ask where moral codes came from, as a naturalist might ask where a species came from. In "What is Noble?" Nietzsche sketches two types. Master morality starts from the self-respect of the strong, who call themselves "good" and the rest "bad." Slave morality starts from the resentment of the weak, who call the strong "evil" and praise humility, pity and patience. He argues that Christianity and modern democracy grew from the second. He developed this a year later in On the Genealogy of Morals.

Nietzsche does not simply say "anything goes." He wants a revaluation of values: philosophers of the future who will question inherited values truthfully and create new ones. He admired self-discipline, honesty with oneself, and the courage to stand alone.

full.text: He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee.
full.author: Nietzsche
full.ed: T. N. Foulis, Edinburgh and London

full.html: Critics answer Nietzsche on several fronts. If every view is only a perspective, so is his own, which seems to undercut it. Many find his praise of the strong careless of the weak, and his remarks on women plainly prejudiced. Religious thinkers reply that he mistakes Christian love for weakness. After his death his sister, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, edited his papers to suit her nationalist and anti-Semitic views, and the Nazis later claimed him. Nietzsche himself despised the anti-Semites of his day and broke with his publisher over them; scholars since Walter Kaufmann (1950) have shown how badly his work was bent.

Reading one shocking aphorism as Nietzsche's whole view. He wrote to provoke, often tried out positions and argued against himself, and in another book asked his readers to read him slowly and carefully.

items: Plato: the Preface calls Plato's "pure spirit and the good in itself" the worst of errors; Nietzsche's whole book is an argument with the idea of a truer world behind this one.
Descartes and Kant: Chapter I questions the certainty of the "I think" and Kant's claims about what the mind supplies.
Darwin: Nietzsche borrowed the idea of a natural history of morals but rejected the Darwinians' focus on mere survival.
Mill and the utilitarians: Nietzsche mocked the aim of comfort and happiness for the greatest number.
Dostoevsky, later in this era, whom Nietzsche read and admired, asked from the other side what happens to morals when faith is lost.
Can we ever step outside our own point of view?
Where do our ideas of good and bad come from? Does knowing their history change whether they are true?
Is humility a strength or a weakness?
What does Nietzsche's warning about monsters and abysses mean in everyday life?

questions: Can you think of something that looks different depending on where you stand?
Why do people often believe what everyone around them believes?
Nietzsche admired people who think for themselves. How can you tell if you are doing that?
"He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he become a monster." Can you think of a story where that happens?
Is it fair to judge a writer by how others misused his books?
